knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2)
library(nlmixr2lib)

library(rxode2)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Model and source

Lei 2017b tests **marbofloxacin**, a veterinary fluoroquinolone, against
*Streptococcus suis* serotype 2 in pigs. Serum was collected after a single
8 mg/kg oral dose, and each serum sample was challenged ex vivo with the
virulent strain HB2. The 24 h change in bacterial count was related to the
PK/PD index AUC0-24h/MIC with an inhibitory sigmoid Emax model fitted in
WinNonlin (equation 1, Table 3, Figure 6).

| Model file | What it is | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `Lei_2017b_marbofloxacin_pkpd_index` | Ex vivo inhibitory sigmoid Emax model, 24 h change in log10 CFU/mL vs AUC0-24h/MIC, pig serum | Equation 1, Table 3, Figure 6 |

The `b` suffix separates this paper from the same group's marbofloxacin
study against *Escherichia coli* in pig ileum content (Lei 2017,
doi:10.3389/fphar.2017.00542), which this paper cites as Lei et al. 2017a.

The pharmacokinetics in the paper are non-compartmental only (Table 1), so no
PK model file is packaged; see *Assumptions and deviations*.

* Article: <https://doi.org/10.3389/fphar.2017.00856>

```{r model}
mod <- rxode2::rxode2(readModelDb("Lei_2017b_marbofloxacin_pkpd_index"))
```

# Population

Eight healthy pigs (four male, four female) received marbofloxacin 8 mg/kg
orally and, after a two-week washout, 8 mg/kg intravenously. Serum was sampled
from 0.25 to 72 h after each dose. The paper gives two descriptions of the
animals: 15-20 kg and 8-10 weeks old (Animals and Treatment) and 16-20 kg and
5-6 weeks old (Animal Study). After the oral dose the serum Cmax was
6.28 ug/mL at 0.75 h, AUC0-24h was 60.30 ug*h/mL and the bioavailability was
94.21% (Table 1). Marbofloxacin was 92% unbound in serum.

*S. suis* HB2 is a virulent serotype 2 pig isolate. Its marbofloxacin MIC is
1 ug/mL in tryptone soya broth and 2 ug/mL in pig serum, which equals the
MIC90 of 134 clinical isolates collected from Chinese pigs in 2016-2017
(Figure 1). In the ex vivo time-kill assay 10^6 CFU/mL of HB2 were cultivated
in each serum sample for 24 h (Figure 3B). The model takes no animal
covariates, so no virtual cohort is needed; every simulation below is a
deterministic typical-value solve.

# Source trace

| Quantity | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Sigmoid Emax equation as printed | `E = Emax*(1 - C^N/(C^N + EC50^N))` | Equation 1 |
| Sigmoid Emax equation as fitted | `E = Emax - (Emax - E0)*C^N/(C^N + EC50^N)` | Table 3 targets, Figure 6 |
| Paper's Emax (drug-free change) -> `e0` | 1.67 log10 CFU/mL | Table 3 |
| Lower plateau E0 -> `emax` | -6.66 log10 CFU/mL (back-solved) | Table 3 targets; Figure 6 |
| EC50 | 33.82 h | Table 3 |
| N (Hill coefficient) | 4.70 | Table 3 |
| Targets for E = 0 / -3 / -4 | 25.23 / 35.64 / 39.71 h | Table 3 |
| MIC of HB2 in serum (`mic`) | 2 ug/mL | Results, MIC/MBC/MPC section; Table 2 ratios |
| Ex vivo inoculum (`log10_cfu0`) | 10^6 CFU/mL | Methods, killing-time curves ex vivo |
| Ex vivo exposure `AUC_MARBOFLOXACIN` | 24 h x sample concentration | Equation 1 definition of C; Figure 6 x range |
| Serum NCA, oral | Cmax 6.28 ug/mL, AUC0-24h 60.30 ug*h/mL, Clb 0.104 L/h, F 94.21% | Table 1 |
| Unbound fraction | 92 +/- 4.3% | Results, PK analysis |
| In vivo AUC0-24h/MIC | 30.06 h | Table 2 |
| Dose equation | `Dose = (AUC/MIC) x MIC90 x CL / (fu x F)` | Methods, Dose Estimations |
| MIC90 of 134 isolates | 2 ug/mL | Results, MIC distribution |
| Predicted daily doses | 5.88 / 8.34 / 9.36 (50%), 8.16 / 11.31 / 12.35 (90%) mg/kg | Table 4, Figure 7 |

# The lower plateau of the effect curve

Equation 1 is printed as `E = Emax*(1 - C^N/(C^N + EC50^N))`. That curve falls
from Emax at zero exposure to 0 at saturation, so it can never produce the
net kill (E = -3 and -4) that Table 3 reports targets for, nor the curve of
Figure 6, which falls from about +1.5 to about -7. The model WinNonlin fitted
is the inhibitory sigmoid form with a lower plateau E0, which is not printed.
With the printed Emax, EC50 and N fixed, each Table 3 target is one equation in
that single unknown:

```{r plateau}
e0_paper <- 1.67
ec50 <- 33.82
hill <- 4.70
tab3 <- data.frame(E = c(0, -3, -4), target = c(25.23, 35.64, 39.71))
frac <- tab3$target^hill / (tab3$target^hill + ec50^hill)
tab3$plateau <- e0_paper - (e0_paper - tab3$E) / frac
plateau_ls <- sum(frac * (tab3$E - e0_paper * (1 - frac))) / sum(frac^2)
tab3 |>
  dplyr::mutate(plateau = round(plateau, 3)) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Target E (log10 CFU/mL)" = E,
    "Published AUC0-24h/MIC (h)" = target,
    "Lower plateau implied (log10 CFU/mL)" = plateau
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Lower plateau of the sigmoid model implied by each Table 3 target.")
round(plateau_ls, 3)
stopifnot(
  # Three independent targets agree on one plateau to within 0.05 log10,
  # so the targets were computed from a single curve with this plateau.
  diff(range(tab3$plateau)) < 0.06,
  abs(plateau_ls - (-6.66)) < 0.005
)
```

The three targets agree on a plateau of -6.62 to -6.67; the least-squares
value, -6.66, is packaged as the fixed `emax`.

# Table 3 target indices

The packaged model is solved over a fine grid of exposures and the 24 h change
is interpolated at each Table 3 target level.

```{r targets}
mic <- 2
cfu0 <- 1e6
grid_aucmic <- exp(seq(log(1), log(1000), length.out = 800))
ex_events <- function(aucmic) {
  data.frame(
    id = seq_along(aucmic), time = 24, evid = 0, amt = 0, cmt = "bact",
    AUC_MARBOFLOXACIN = aucmic * mic
  )
}
sim_grid <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod, ex_events(grid_aucmic), returnType = "data.frame")
# The 24 h change is read from the bacterial state itself; the `log_cfu`
# output adds a 1 CFU/mL floor that biases it near the maximal kill.
dE <- log10(sim_grid$bact) - log10(cfu0)

targets <- data.frame(
  E = c(0, -3, -4),
  published = c(25.23, 35.64, 39.71)
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    model = approx(dE, grid_aucmic, xout = E)$y,
    pct_diff = 100 * (model - published) / published
  )
targets |>
  dplyr::mutate(model = round(model, 2), pct_diff = round(pct_diff, 2)) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Target E (log10 CFU/mL)" = E,
    "Published AUC0-24h/MIC (h)" = published,
    "Model AUC0-24h/MIC (h)" = model,
    "Difference (%)" = pct_diff
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Table 3 target indices, published versus solved from the packaged model.")
```

```{r targets-check}
stopifnot(
  # The plateau was solved from these targets, so they must come back;
  # the residual is the rounding of the printed parameters.
  all(abs(targets$pct_diff) < 0.5)
)
```

# Ex vivo ODE versus the closed-form equation

The model integrates the bacterial density so that its log10 changes by exactly
the sigmoid value over 24 h. Both sides use the same parameters, so the
difference is pure numerical error and is held to a tight bound.

```{r ode-check}
closed_form <- function(x, top = 1.67, bottom = -6.66, c50 = 33.82, n = 4.70) {
  top - (top - bottom) * x^n / (x^n + c50^n)
}
stopifnot(
  all(abs(dE - closed_form(grid_aucmic)) < 1e-3),
  # Drug-free control and saturation.
  abs(closed_form(0) - 1.67) < 1e-12,
  abs(dE[length(dE)] - (-6.66)) < 1e-2
)
```

# Effect curve (replicates Figure 6)

Figure 6 is a small raster image. Its drawn curve was digitised by the
maintainers (the blue pixels of each column, mapped through the axis ticks)
and a sigmoid was fitted to the trace: Emax 1.35, lower plateau -7.04,
EC50 33.81 h and N 4.72. EC50 and N match Table 3 to within 0.3%; the two
plateaus do not, which is discussed below.

```{r fig6, fig.cap = "Replicates Figure 6 of Lei 2017b: 24 h change in S. suis HB2 count versus ex vivo AUC0-24h/MIC. Solid: packaged model (Table 3 parameters with the back-solved plateau). Dashed: sigmoid fitted to the digitised Figure 6 curve. Points: Table 3 targets."}
drawn <- c(top = 1.35, bottom = -7.04, c50 = 33.81, n = 4.72)
curves <- data.frame(aucmic = grid_aucmic, model = dE) |>
  dplyr::filter(aucmic <= 80) |>
  dplyr::mutate(drawn = closed_form(aucmic, drawn[["top"]], drawn[["bottom"]], drawn[["c50"]], drawn[["n"]]))
ggplot(curves, aes(aucmic)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = model), linewidth = 1, colour = "navy") +
  geom_line(aes(y = drawn), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey30") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0, -3, -4), linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(data = targets, aes(published, E), colour = "firebrick", size = 2.5) +
  labs(x = "AUC0-24h/MIC (h)", y = "Change in log10 CFU/mL over 24 h") +
  theme_bw()
```

```{r fig6-check}
stopifnot(
  # The digitised curve and Table 3 share the midpoint and steepness.
  abs(drawn[["c50"]] / 33.82 - 1) < 0.01,
  abs(drawn[["n"]] / 4.70 - 1) < 0.01,
  # Largest index plotted in Figure 6 (about 75 h) is the mean serum Cmax.
  abs(6.28 * 24 / mic - 75.4) < 0.1
)
```

The packaged curve runs about 0.3 log10 above the drawn one on the drug-free
plateau and 0.4 log10 above it at saturation, while crossing the half-way
point at the same index. Using the drawn plateaus would move the Table 3
targets 1-3% lower (24.90 / 34.88 / 38.62 h with Table 3 Emax and the drawn
lower plateau), so the paper's targets and doses were not computed from the
drawn curve.

# Exposure after the 8 mg/kg oral dose

Table 2 integrates the in vivo serum AUC0-24h with the serum MIC to give an
AUC0-24h/MIC of 30.06 h (60.30 / 2 = 30.15 from the Table 1 mean). The paper
concludes that the 8 mg/kg dose falls short of a bactericidal effect. The
model places that exposure at about a 1.4 log10 kill, between the
bacteriostatic (0) and bactericidal (-3) levels.

```{r in-vivo-index}
sim_iv <- rxode2::rxSolve(
  mod,
  data.frame(id = 1, time = 24, evid = 0, amt = 0, cmt = "bact", AUC_MARBOFLOXACIN = 60.12),
  returnType = "data.frame"
)
change_iv <- log10(sim_iv$bact) - log10(cfu0)
round(change_iv, 2)
stopifnot(
  abs(60.30 / mic - 30.06) < 0.1,
  change_iv < -1.2, change_iv > -1.6
)
```

# Predicted daily doses (Table 4)

The dose equation `Dose = (AUC/MIC) x MIC90 x CL / (fu x F)` was evaluated with
MIC90 = 2 ug/mL (Figure 1), the oral clearance Clb = 0.104 L/h per kg body
weight (Table 1), fu = 0.92 and F = 0.9421. Evaluated at the mean inputs it
gives doses 1.8-3% above the Table 4 50% column. Table 4 is the median and 90th
percentile of a Crystal Ball Monte Carlo (Figure 7 shows the dose
histograms). The paper does not state which inputs were sampled; drawing the
target, Clb and fu from normal distributions with their printed SDs (Table 3,
Table 1 and the protein-binding result) reproduces Table 4 closely. Base R's
random number generator is used here, so the draw is the same on every
machine.

```{r doses}
mic90 <- 2
clb <- 0.104
fu <- 0.92
f_oral <- 0.9421
model_targets <- targets$model
target_sd <- c(4.25, 4.85, 6.45)
set.seed(20171124)
n_mc <- 1e5
mc <- lapply(seq_along(model_targets), function(i) {
  dose <- rnorm(n_mc, model_targets[i], target_sd[i]) * mic90 *
    rnorm(n_mc, clb, 0.02) / (rnorm(n_mc, fu, 0.043) * f_oral)
  stats::quantile(dose, c(0.5, 0.9), names = FALSE)
})
doses <- data.frame(
  endpoint = c("Bacteriostatic (E = 0)", "Bactericidal (E = -3)", "Elimination (E = -4)"),
  at_mean = model_targets * mic90 * clb / (fu * f_oral),
  mc50 = vapply(mc, `[`, numeric(1), 1),
  pub50 = c(5.88, 8.34, 9.36),
  mc90 = vapply(mc, `[`, numeric(1), 2),
  pub90 = c(8.16, 11.31, 12.35)
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    pct50 = 100 * (mc50 - pub50) / pub50,
    pct90 = 100 * (mc90 - pub90) / pub90
  )
doses |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(at_mean, mc50, mc90, pct50, pct90), \(x) round(x, 2))) |>
  dplyr::select(endpoint, at_mean, pub50, mc50, pct50, pub90, mc90, pct90) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Endpoint" = endpoint,
    "Dose at mean inputs" = at_mean,
    "Monte Carlo 50%" = mc50, "Table 4 50%" = pub50, "Difference 50% (%)" = pct50,
    "Monte Carlo 90%" = mc90, "Table 4 90%" = pub90, "Difference 90% (%)" = pct90
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Table 4 daily doses (mg/kg) versus the dose equation driven by the model-solved targets.")
```

```{r doses-check}
stopifnot(
  # Mean inputs sit 1.8-3% above the Monte Carlo medians of Table 4.
  all(doses$at_mean / doses$pub50 > 1.01 & doses$at_mean / doses$pub50 < 1.04),
  # The Monte Carlo reproduces the medians and the 90th percentiles; a
  # mis-read MIC90 (1 instead of 2) would halve every dose.
  all(abs(doses$pct50) < 2.5),
  all(abs(doses$pct90) < 5)
)
```

# PKNCA

There is no PKNCA section. The packaged model has no pharmacokinetic state: the
paper reports only a non-compartmental analysis of the serum concentrations
(Table 1) and no structural PK model, so there is no simulated
concentration-time profile to analyse. The exposure that drives the model is
supplied as the `AUC_MARBOFLOXACIN` covariate.

# Assumptions and deviations

* **Equation 1 and the lower plateau.** Equation 1 is printed without its lower
  plateau, which makes the Table 3 net-kill targets unreachable. The model uses
  the inhibitory sigmoid form with the plateau E0 back-solved from the three
  Table 3 targets at the printed Emax, EC50 and N. The three targets agree to
  within 0.05 log10 (-6.62, -6.65, -6.67) and the least-squares value -6.66 is
  fixed in the model. It is not a published estimate.
* **Emax and E0 naming.** The paper's Emax is the drug-free change (+1.67,
  growth), and the curve falls with exposure. The model maps the paper's Emax
  onto the canonical `e0` and the lower plateau onto the canonical `emax`. No
  printed value is changed.
* **Figure 6 versus Table 3.** A sigmoid fitted to the digitised Figure 6 curve
  has the Table 3 EC50 and N but plateaus of about +1.35 and -7.04 rather than
  +1.67 and -6.66. The Table 3 targets and the Table 4 doses follow the Table 3
  parameters, not the drawn curve, so the model packages the Table 3
  parameters. The drawn plateaus are shown for comparison only.
* **No PK model.** Lei 2017b analysed the pharmacokinetics non-compartmentally
  only and reports no volume or absorption rate. The intravenous clearance and
  rate constant (0.085 L/h/kg and 0.046 1/h) imply an apparent volume of about
  1.85 L/kg, and 8 mg/kg x 0.94 spread over that volume is about 4.1 ug/mL,
  below the observed oral Cmax of 6.28 ug/mL even with instantaneous
  absorption, so a one-compartment model cannot be reconstructed from Table 1.
  The exposure is therefore supplied as a covariate, as in the paper's own
  PK/PD integration.
* **Clearance units.** Table 1 reports Clb in L/h. The Table 4 doses come out
  in mg/kg only if it is per kg body weight, and 8 mg/kg / 88.94 ug*h/mL =
  0.090 L/h/kg is of the same size, so per kg is assumed.
* **MIC90.** The Abstract gives an MIC90 of 1 ug/mL for the 134 isolates; the
  Results give MIC50 1 and MIC90 2 ug/mL. The Table 4 doses require MIC90 =
  2 ug/mL (with 1 ug/mL every dose halves), so 2 is used in the dose check.
  MIC90 does not enter the model.
* **MIC of HB2.** The model uses the serum MIC, 2 ug/mL, because the index is
  formed in serum; the Table 2 ratios (Cmax/MIC = 6.28/2 = 3.14,
  AUC0-24h/MIC = 30.06, close to 60.30/2) and the Figure 6 x range require it.
  The in vitro killing curves were set up on the broth MIC of 1 ug/mL.
* **Bioavailability.** Results and Table 1 give 94.21%, which equals the ratio
  of the oral and intravenous AUC0-inf (88.94 / 94.40); the Discussion gives
  97.74%. The Table 1 value is used in the dose check.
* **Animals.** The two Methods paragraphs describe the same eight pigs with
  different weight and age ranges (15-20 kg, 8-10 weeks versus 16-20 kg,
  5-6 weeks). Both are recorded; neither enters the model.
* **Ex vivo inoculum.** The ex vivo time-kill design states 10^6 CFU/mL; that
  value is used for `log10_cfu0`. The predicted 24 h change does not depend on
  it.
* **Variability.** Table 3 reports mean +/- SD of the estimates; no
  between-animal variance or residual error was estimated, so the model has no
  random effects and `addSd` is fixed at 0. The Monte Carlo check above uses
  the printed SDs outside the model.
* **Errata.** No erratum or correction to Lei 2017b was found, and the article
  has no supplementary material beyond its figures (Europe PMC, checked
  2026-11-25).
